items.title: In Canada: Canada Music Fund to Receive $67M Boost; Women in Music Executive Award Winners Share Their Wisdom
items.summary:
The Canada Music Fund is getting a new boost from the federal government.

At last night’s ADISQ Gala in Montreal (Nov. 8), the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture, Marc Miller, announced that the federal government will invest $67 million to the Canada Music Fund, as part of the government’s promised $600 million investment into the cultural sector. The sum was first announced in June to provide “immediate relief” to the country’s audio and audiovisual sector and confirmed for 2026-27 in the latest federal budget , which was tabled last week. Over the weekend, Ottawa gave a long-awaited breakdown of how the funds will be allocated.

Related 

Canadian Government Introduces Canada Creative Credit to Support ‘Artistic Production’ 

CL Signs With THEBLACKLABEL, Reuniting With Longtime Producer Teddy For 'Full Circle' Moment 

Severe Weather, Radius Clauses and Finding the Next Generation of Festival Headliners: 'It's a Year-by-Year Fight to Stay Alive' 

The music sector will receive its share of the relief investment through the Canada Music Fund, which was renewed through 2028 last year . The $67 million sum will be distributed to the five organizations that the fund supports, with FACTOR (Foundation Assisting Canadian Talent on Recordings) receiving $31.5 million, Musicaction (which funds and supports Francophone music and music companies) receiving $21 million, the Canadian Starmaker Fund receiving $5.7 million, the RadioStar fund receiving $3.8 million and the Indigenous Music Office (IMO) receiving $5 million.

Last November, the IMO released a new national…

The 2027 College Football Playoff National Championship will see two top teams competing on Jan. 25 at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas. Before that, a heavy-hitting lineup of DJs will provide pump-up music before the big game. 

This year’s edition of AT&T Playoff Playlist Live – The CFP Music Festival will happen Jan. 23-24 at Las Vegas’ Grand Prix Plaza, located just off the Strip. Admission to this event is free, with advance registration required. Registration details will be announced via the CFP’s official mobile app at a later date.

“No city embraces the variety of music genres like Las Vegas,” Ryan Allen Hall, the CFP senior director of public events and sponsorships, says in a statement. “But it’s clear, electronic music is the pulse. From the residencies, nightclubs, dayclubs, lounges, pools and festivals, the city simply does EDM like only a select few in the entire world. 

“But the magic for us is to bring together this stacked lineup in Las Vegas and to charge the fans absolutely nothing,” Hall continues. “It is all part of the CFP’s commitment to providing a world class championship experience to our fans and guests, especially during National Championship week. items.title: Il Volo Reflect on 18 Years Together, Their Christmas Traditions and What’s Next
items.summary:
“Did you go to their concert? I really like them,” Gianluca asks me when he spots my Fontaines D.C. tote bag on the set of the cover shoot. The Irish band’s concert in Bologna took place just a week earlier, and it is in the same city that we meet Il Volo for this interview, shortly before the release of the album Our Christmas and ahead of their upcoming tour, which will take them across the United States and to some of Italy’s biggest arenas.

The fact that one of the members of the world’s most famous Italian trio is a fan of one of the world’s most popular rock bands is just the first of many surprises we encounter while spending an afternoon with Gianluca, Piero and Ignazio. On stages around the globe, we are used to seeing them as impeccably elegant ambassadors of classical singing. Away from the spotlight, however, they are perfectly ordinary guys in their early thirties, with passions, a sense of humor and a desire to have fun that make them far more relatable to their peers than one might imagine.

What really strikes you when watching them in action – whether in front of a video camera or a photographer – is just how well-oiled a machine they have become after 18 years together. Every movement is perfectly rehearsed, and their chemistry is so natural that each seems to instinctively complete the other’s thoughts.

After a photoshoot in which we asked them to pose in some rather unconventional outfits (at least in terms of their public image), they say that the real secret to staying together for so long is trust. “If one of us speaks on behalf of all three, the…
items.t: Il Volo Reflect on 18 Years Together, Their Christmas Traditions and What’s Next

items.title: Viva La Lisa! 5 Best Moments From LISA’s Opening Night in Las Vegas
items.summary:
Las Vegas has new residency royalty: queen LISA .

The BLACKPINK rapper, singer and dancer became the first K-pop artist to headline a Las Vegas residency Thursday night (Nov. 12), opening her six-show “Viva La Lisa” engagement at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace with a fast-paced, 90-minute production, high-energy choreography and enough costume changes to fill a showgirl’s dressing room.

Related 

Lisa’s ‘Viva La Lisa’ Las Vegas Residency Setlist: Every Song From Night 1 

The Thai-born superstar, who made her solo Coachella debut in 2025 and appeared in season 3 of HBO’s The White Lotus , has plenty of material to work with. Her debut solo album, Alter Ego , arrived in February 2025, followed by the six-track EP Press Play on Oct. 23. She performed the entire EP — including several live debuts — along with established solo hits, collaborations, and one previously unreleased song.

Each chapter of “Viva” presented a facet of LISA’s stage persona, from a crimson-clad goddess emerging from a lotus blossom to a futuristic provocateur, a playful pop star and a dark angel. Using a multi-level stage, aerial apparatuses, and a hydraulic satellite stage, LISA met her fans where they were — sometimes even at eye level — while the production moved between cinematic fantasy, club culture, and Thai imagery.

Here are five of the best moments from opening night.
items.t: Viva La Lisa! 5 Best Moments From LISA’s Opening Night in Las Vegas

items.title: Drake Finally Makes ‘Take Care’ Bonus Track ‘Hate Sleeping Alone’ Available Across All Streaming Platforms
items.summary:
Drake ‘s genre-shifting sophomore album Take Care turns 11 this weekend (Nov. 15), and to celebrate, he made a fan-favorite loosie/bonus track available on all streaming platforms, with an emphasis on YouTube and Spotify.

Produced by Noah “40” Shebib and featuring background vocals from Trey Songz , “Hate Sleeping Alone” was originally made exclusively available as a bonus track on Take Care ‘s digital edition alongside the Lil Wayne -assisted “The Motto.” Fans are noticeably hyped judging by the comments on YouTube. “This song is the only reason I’ve been using Apple Music for the past five years,” one fan wrote. “Most underrated song in drakes discography I used to pray for times like this,” while another added, “Let’s go, this finally released on Spotify,” in all caps.

The song features the Toronto rapper’s signature style from that era as he seamlessly switches from rapping to singing while lamenting about having to sleep alone over 40’s moody production. “I say I’d rather be with you, but you are not around,” Drake sings on the chorus. “So I’ma call somebody up and see if they’d be down/ ‘Cause I hate sleepin’ alone, I hate sleepin’ alone.”

Speaking of his Take Care era, Drake recently found himself singing along to the title track — which featured Rihanna and went top 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 — on a Kick livestream. He told fans that he’ll probably never perform that song again . “This the only performance you’re getting of this song probably, but s–t, welcome to Trainwreckstv, baby,” he said to the chat.

Check out “Hate Sleeping Alone” below.
items.t: Drake Finally Makes ‘Take Care’ Bonus Track ‘Hate Sleeping Alone’ Available Across All Streaming Platforms

items.title: Rosalía makes history with Album Of The Year award win at Latin Grammys and performs ‘Lux’ medley
items.summary:
Rosalía has made history at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards, winning Album Of The Year for the third time and playing a medley of songs from ‘Lux’ – watch below.

READ MORE: Rosalía live in London: a breathtakingly brilliant work of art 

The Spanish star was among the biggest winners at the 27th annual ceremony, which took place at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas last night (November 12).

She claimed the night’s biggest prize for ‘Lux (Complete Works)’, becoming the first woman to win Album Of The Year three times as a lead artist, following her previous victories for ‘El Mal Querer’ in 2019 and ‘Motomami’ in 2022.

The achievement places her alongside Alejandro Sanz and Juanes, who have also won the category three times. Only Juan Luis Guerra has won it more often, with four victories.

Rosalía was visibly emotional as she accepted the award from Juanes, recalling how the Colombian musician had supported her at the beginning of her career, attending concerts in Madrid when she was performing to audiences of around 100 people.

Addressing the audience in Spanish, she reflected on the creative risks behind her three award-winning albums.

“This is the third time I’ve won this award, and — just as ‘El Mal Querer’ felt like a dream, or ‘Motomami’ was a gamble — ‘Lux’ has been, for me, a leap into the void,” she said.

“I believe it’s very important to speak your own truth and for others to be able to speak theirs; this album is my truth.”

She also thanked the people who had supported her artistic vision, as well as reflecting on those who had previously dismissed her…
items.t: Rosalía makes history with Album Of The Year award win at Latin Grammys and performs ‘Lux’ medley

items.title: Blink-182’s Travis Barker quit smoking after being “diagnosed with precancer of the oesophagus”
items.summary:
Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker has revealed that he quit smoking after being diagnosed with precancer of the oesophagus.

During a recent episode of the Big Bro With Kid Cudi podcast, the musician opened up about the time he decided to adopt a “healthier” lifestyle over 20 years ago.

READ MORE:  Blink-182 – ‘One More Time’ review: a surprisingly touching reunion 

“I was like, ‘Oh, man, I’m having a son,” he said, referring to his first son, Landon, born in 2003. “So I started running to the freeway and back. I didn’t really know what I was doing – I was just like, ‘I gotta be healthy, I gotta be a badass dad!”

Barker went on to recall his past decision to “start balancing out” some of his “bad” habits with the “good” ones. He said getting more exercise also “helped [him] stay sober” from drugs.

“My running started getting bigger and more important to me than smoking,” he continued. “[…] It’s like therapy.”

As for his decision to stop smoking weed and cigarettes altogether, Barker shared: “I only quit because I got diagnosed with precancer of the oesophagus. ‘Cause I loved blunts and I would smoke too much. So that was the only [reason].”

The drummer said he asked his doctor if he was “serious” about the diagnosis. “He’s like, ‘This is your warning shot, Trav. Don’t fuck around. You’ve got to stop smoking’. Or I would’ve never stopped.

“I thought I could be like Willie Nelson and smoke to the day I die, you know?”.

But the drummer admitted that he still “misses” smoking. Watch the full interview in the video above.

READ MORE: U2: “You have to up your game when people step into the room like Fontaines D.C.” 

The emotional ballad closes U2’s 16th studio album ‘Carnaval De Luz’ , which is out today (November 13), and features the late country star trading vocals with Bono .

An alternative recording, titled ‘Torn (Kent Wells Version)’, also arrived today, having received its premiere on US country radio yesterday (November 12). The version takes a more traditional country approach to the song, in contrast to the atmospheric arrangement on U2’s album.

The two recordings offer contrasting settings for Parton’s final vocal performance, with her distinctive voice at the centre of a song about family relationships fractured by political divisions.

Listen to both versions of ‘Torn’ here:

Speaking to The Sun , Bono explained the differences between the recordings, saying: “We did something similar with Johnny Cash. If you think about Larry’s drum part, it’s more of a sci-fi country landscape.”

“I think he did her a favour by not doing the obvious but it was risky. If she didn’t run with it — and she’d have no problem telling you — then we’d have lost her.

“But she liked the direction we took it and her camp has a more traditional country version, which they’re going to put out.

“Hearing her voice in the context of ‘Carnaval De Luz’ is a bit of a shock and a welcome one.”

items.title: Violet Grohl shares “dystopian” new song ‘Metal Birds’ from ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’
items.summary:
Violet Grohl has shared a new song, ‘Metal Birds’, from the soundtrack to The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping . Listen below.

The slow-burning, atmospheric track arrived today (Friday November 13), ahead of the sixth film in the Hunger Games franchise, which hits cinemas on November 20.

It marks the first material from Grohl since dropping her acclaimed debut studio album, ‘Be Sweet To Me’ , in May.

“Writing ‘Metal Birds’ was one of the most special songwriting experiences for me,” she explained. “I’ve loved the [ Hunger Games ] movies and the book series since I was a kid, so it was a total honour to be asked to write a song about a story that I feel so connected to.

“It opened up the world of dystopian themes for me. I found the visuals in the movie to be so striking and strong and important to the plot that I felt like I needed to include them in the song.”

She added: “And I took mental notes of lots of things I had seen, and they really stuck with me. And so the songwriting process came really easily and was really fun.”

Produced by Justin Raisen and Lewis Pesacov, ‘Metal Birds’ finds Grohl singing over a moody, stripped-back instrumental: “ Metal birds in the sky/ Come and take me away/ Generator, power breaker / Look at me through the embers .”

Later in the song, the simple electric guitar work is accompanied by some increasingly lush orchestral elements. “ Kiss you with a smile/ Death hung around my neck ,” Grohl adds. “ Let’s leave it for a while/ I’ll lay the flowers on your chest/ Open eyes are for the weeping .”

Out today, ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise…

items.title: Philharmonia/Honeck/Ax review – principal conductor designate gives a scorching taste of things to come
items.summary:
Royal Festival Hall, London
With this programme of Strauss (Johann II and Richard) and Mozart – and Emanuel Ax the deft and lucid soloist – Manfred Honeck, who joins as principal conductor in 2028, gave an exciting statement of intent

‘I am a man of tradition,” Manfred Honeck, the Philharmonia’s new principal conductor designate, declared earlier this week in rehearsals. But for the 68-year-old Austrian, who in 2028 becomes only the seventh principal conductor in the ensemble’s 81-year history, it’s tradition as defined by Mahler: “Not the worship of the ashes but the preservation of fire.” It was a fire in full blaze by the end of last night’s concert – a scorching taste of things to come.

Even if you couldn’t see Honeck smiling at his musicians, or them smiling back, you could hear it in a Fledermaus Overture that could barely keep the mischievous grin from its face. Conducting from memory, Honeck (a former violist) brought a decade of New Year’s Day concerts with the Vienna Philharmonic to bear on the sleek drape of the strings and the patent-leather gleam of woodwind, the elegance of those artfully delayed final beats of the bar tempering the madcap scuttle of the semiquavers.

Continue reading...
items.t: Philharmonia/Honeck/Ax review – principal conductor designate gives a scorching taste of things to come

items.title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month
items.summary:
(Erased Tapes)
Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation

Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr, in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir.

On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. The resulting atmosphere sits somewhere between PJ Harvey’s late-90s eerie grunge and the trip-hop qawwali of Massive Attack’s work with singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan – an ambience that is…
items.t: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month

Boris Kor Tom Zeebroek is staring up at a grey gothic building in the centre of Ghent, squinting through the late September sun that is covering his home town in a cloak of unseasonal warmth.

Zeebroek is encouraging his bandmate Charlotte Adigéry and I to crane our necks towards the Mammelokker, an 18th-century Flemish relief on the top of the building. It’s a gruesome bit of stone, which sits above the town square and depicts a daughter suckling her own father. The pair are taking me on a tour of their medieval home town, and this disturbing architectural decoration is part of our itinerary.

items.title: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis
items.summary:
The band’s uneven 2003 album has been judiciously reworked to accompany a staging of Shakespeare’s tragedy with quite extraordinary results

According to the programme notes, Thom Yorke had serious reservations about director Christine Jones’ idea to stage a production of Hamlet featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief. Who can blame him? Many criticisms have been laid at Radiohead’s door but being hopelessly naff isn’t one of them, and, alas, naff is very much the adjective you’d apply to a lot of attempts to meld Shakespeare and rock music.

You’re often in the realm of high camp – portentous, Bard-quoting heavy metal lyrics; Return to the Forbidden Planet’s jokey blending of The Tempest with 50s rock’n’roll; 2015’s These Paper Bullets, which relocated Much Ado About Nothing to swinging London, complete with Beatle-y songs by Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong – or of buttock-clenching disasters like Catch My Soul, a 1971 rock adaptation of Othello which required Black American soul singer PP Arnold to star opposite impresario Jack Good, playing the title role in blackface.

Continue…
items.t: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis

items.title: ‘Joni Mitchell sang Both Sides, Now over the phone to me’: folk music legend Judy Collins on her 87 remarkable years
items.summary:
As she continues her farewell tour, the US singer-songwriter answers your questions on romance with Stephen Stills, friendship with Carly Simon and how folk underpins all pop

How did you come into Joni Mitchell’s orbit and how did you end up recording Both Sides, Now before she did? Steve-bayley
I’m 48 years sober, but in the old days I drank. One night in 1967, I was passed out and the phone rang at about 3am. It was my friend [the musician, songwriter and producer] Al Kooper. He said he’d been at a club and had run into this woman, Joni, who wrote songs. He put her on the phone and she sang Both Sides, Now over the phone. It was brilliant. I said: “I’ll be right over.” I recorded it the next day and it became a huge hit.

I don’t think Joni was too happy that I was the first to record it, but she was very generous and I’ve since recorded many of her songs. She was unknown then, so I’m proud that I was able to help introduce her to the world. She’s one of the great writers of all time.

items.title: Blackhaine: Saints in the Wethouse review | Alexis Petridis's album of the week
items.summary:
(XL Recordings)
His Playboi Carti collabs may have dragged Tom Heyes out of the underground, but this bracing debut remains far from the mainstream, full of garbled barks and walls of noise

On the second track on his debut album, Tom Heyes accuses lesser artists of copying him. “What the fuck you even take me for?” he barks on Northside Needs Me, over a grinding, distorted bassline that comes punctuated with stammering, rave-y vocal samples. “Too much noise shit, replicating what I played before.”

Of course, charging that others are merely imitating what you did previously is a venerable rap tradition: the track that gave said practice its longstanding name, Bite’n My Stylee by Original Concept, is now 40 years old. Perhaps it’s true that others have been copying the approach that Heyes has minted under the alias of Blackhaine, but if so, it seems faintly remarkable, because his approach is so determinedly unique.

items.title: ‘Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard’: ​from football to Top Boy and wordplay, the inspiring journey of UK rapper Cristale
items.summary:
Crystal Palace FC or Oxbridge beckoned, but the multitalented MC kept forging her way towards music. She explains how she poured every aspect of herself into her debut mixtape

Two weeks before we meet, UK rapper Cristale was scrambling down a cliff face to a secluded black pebbled beach in Dover, racing an incoming tide with fewer than 90 minutes to shoot the video for her single I’m Okay With Being Lonely. She’d never hiked before in her life. “I was wearing head-to-toe Stone Island, no hiking gear, full face of makeup, edges laid and Mum was doing my touch-ups on a rusty ladder,” she laughs.

As we sit in her publicist’s central London office, her hair half-braided and half-flowing past a black puffer coat, she says the rush of adrenaline hasn’t fully faded. In fact she seems to thrive on regular bumps of it: beyond her relentlessly articulate and energetic rap flow – put to work on tracks that span drill, introspective R&B and beyond – she has ably hopped between football, art, acting in Netflix projects and more.

items.title: ‘My partners would all tell you I was a nut job’: Jane Wiedlin on the Go-Go’s, fame and the freedom of sex dungeons
items.summary:
As she releases a brutally honest memoir, the new wave icon opens up about industry sexism, living with bipolar disorder and becoming ‘the world’s first atheist ordained minister’

The first thing Jane Wiedlin tells me before our interview even begins is that, an hour or so earlier, she downed two beers. “It keeps me cheerful,” she says with a laugh. The disclosure dovetails with the reason we’re doing the interview in the first place, which is to unpack her new memoir, a tome that deserves a truth-in-advertising award for its title alone: TMI (as in “too much information”). “I’ve always been TMI!” Wiedlin proudly announces. “I’m the one who always wanted to expose the truth. This book is my first opportunity to do so.”

A portion of that truth has to do with the band she helped form in the late 70s, the Go-Go’s. The five-piece are not only the first all-female band who play their own instruments and write their own material to earn a No 1 album in the US but, astonishingly, are the only such group to hold that distinction nearly 45 years later. The group’s power-pop music, heard in zippy hits like Our Lips Are Sealed and Vacation, led to their induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021, inspired a Broadway play and influenced modern female artists all the way from Olivia Rodrigo to Wet Leg.

items.t: ‘My partners would all tell you I was a nut job’: Jane Wiedlin on the Go-Go’s, fame and the freedom of sex dungeons

items.title: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
items.summary:
(Island)
On their first album of new songs in nearly a decade, even earnest Bono-isms carry weight amid music that is impassioned and rejuvenated

Even artists who enjoy a seemingly unstoppable imperial period eventually seem to encounter spells of turbulence when the creative planets no longer align – which has been the story of U2’s last 20 years. Try as they might, nothing has matched their earlier albums – especially that mostly uninterrupted golden run from their 1980 debut Boy to 90s benchmarks Achtung Baby and Zooropa.

They’ve tried going more pop, becoming more experimental, touring 1987 colossus The Joshua Tree again and even reworking old songs for 2023’s Songs of Surrender, but nothing has uncorked the genie again, or given the band the kind of relevance they had for so many years. Often, it felt as though they were trying too hard.

items.title: ‘I didn’t dance until I was 45’: how Jorge Drexler went from repressed doctor to rump-shaking Oscar-winner
items.summary:
How did a Uruguayan medic who grew up under an anti-music dictatorship win a best song Academy award? As he looks set to scoop up more prizes at the Latin Grammys, we meet the extraordinary Jorge Drexler

It makes sense that a Uruguayan doctor turned singer would write a song that begins: “Long live science! Long live poetry!” Guitar y Vos (Guitar and You) is also the first track that Jorge Drexler performs this afternoon at a music industry event in the basement of Madrid’s Movistar arena. The second is El Otro Lado del Rio (The Other Side of the River), which he composed for the Che Guevara road movie The Motorcycle Diaries. Drexler was still largely unknown when it won the best original song Oscar in 2005, so was not invited to perform at the ceremony. In a classy act of defiance, he delivered a short a cappella version in lieu of an acceptance speech.

That’s how he sings it today too, solo under a spotlight on the stairs, before joining his band on stage. Backed by three drummers playing in the Afro-Uruguayan candombe style, Drexler turns a corporate lunchtime gig into a midnight block party. From his latest album Taracá – nominated for eight Latin Grammys at the forthcoming awards on 12 November – comes Ante la Duda, Baila (When in Doubt, Dance). While his lyrics list Spanish kings and colonial governments who have banned various forms of dancing over the centuries, the singer duly shakes his ass and moves us to do the same.
items.t: ‘I didn’t dance until I was 45’: how Jorge Drexler went from repressed doctor to rump-shaking Oscar-winner
